lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam with Mafuza Begum, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Md Fazlul Karim with ABM Mahbub, Advocates ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Nurul Haque (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Anowara Begum and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J : This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and decree dated 27-7-1993 decree signed on 31-5-1993 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Title Appeal No.19 of 1992 reversing the judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992, decree signed on 3-6- 1992 passed by the Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon in other Suit No.5 of 1985 should not be set aside.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that, one Mossammat Anowara Begum instituted the Other Suit No.18 of 1980 on 5-2-1980 in the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, Dinajpur praying for setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 declaring the same illegal. collusive and not binding upon her and the learned Munsif by his judgment and decree dated 30-1-1982 has been pleased to decree the suit on contest with costs declaring the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant No.1, namely, Nurul Haque, on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 is not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. As against the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred the Other Appeal No.24 of 1992 and on 14-6-1984 the appeal was allowed by the learned appellate Court, by its Judgment and decree, setting aside the Judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and remanding the suit back to the trial Court with direction to the Learned Munsif to give an opportunity to the plaintiff to amend her plaint. On 25-2-1985 the case record was received by the trial Court from the appellate Court back on remand and the learned trial Court returned the plaint to the plaintiff for filling it before an appropriate Court and the 'plaintiff has re-filed it by amending the plaint in the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon and the suit has been registered as the Other Suit No.5 of 1984 and during trial of the case neither party adduced any additional evidence, but relied upon the evidence recorded earlier in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980.

4. On conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon has been pleased to dismiss the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992 and being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff has preferred the Title Appeal No.19 of 1992 and by judgment and decree dated 27-5-1993 the learned Additional District Judge. Thakurgaon, has been pleased to allow the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and declaring the ex parte decree passed in the Other Class Suit No.1 00 of 1978 on 24-5-1979. by the learned Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon illegal, void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff- appellant also declaring the title of the plaintiff in the suit property directing the defendant No.1 to vacate the suit land by demolishing and removing structures and declaring also khas possession of the plaintiff in the suit land on eviction of the defendant No.1 as aforesaid.

5. As against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Title (Other) Appeal No.19 of 1992 the defendant-respondent has preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule together with an order of stay of all further proceedings of the Title Execution Case No.5 of 1993 pending in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Thakurgaon.

6. Facts as appears from the pleadings of the parties and the judgments of the Courts below are that in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980 the plaintiff Mossammat Anowara Begum stated that the suit land originally belonged to one Subarna Probha Biswas and the CS Khatian No.420 was finally published in her name. Subsequently, the suit property was put to auction in the Certificate Case No.15311958-59 and she along with the defendant No.3 namely, Hanuman Das Agarwala purchased the entire land of the suit Khatian on auction held on 9-11-1959, with equal shares. The sale was confirmed on 9-1-1960 and they got delivery of possession of the suit land from the Court on 16-2-1960 and thus they acquired the right, title interests and possession of the suit land extinguishing the interests of Subarna Probha Biswas.

The defendant No.3 Hanuman Das Agarwala sold his half share to one Upendra Nath Barman who subsequently, filed a Partition Suit in the Court of Munsif: Thakurgaon, Dinajpur being No.143 of 1960 against the plaintiff and her husband and the suit was dismissed on contest. An appeal was preferred being Partition Appeal No.68 of 1961 and the learned Subordinate Judge. Dinajpur was also pleased to dismiss the appeal on contest.

Thereafter, Upendra Nath Barman again filed the Title Suit No.4 of 1963 in the same Court and obtained an ex parte decree on 2-9-1963. The present plaintiff, Mossammat Anowara Begum has then filed a suit for cancellation of that ex parte decree being the Other Suit No.37 of 1966 in the same Court and the said ex parte decree has been set aside and the original suit was restored to its original file and number and Upendra Nath ultimately, obtained a decree in that Title Suit.

The defendant No.1 in the present suit namely, Nurul Haque, was also a defendant in that Title Suit instituted by Upendra Nath Barman.

The defendant No.1. Nurul Haque was at the time residing in the suit land as a rental tenant of this plaintiff: The plaintiff then preferred an appeal against that decree passed in favour of Upendra Nath Barman being the Other Appeal No.31 of 1968 and the learned Subordinate Judge. Dinajpur has been pleased to dismiss the appeal. Ultimately, the present plaintiff Mossammat Anowara Begum, purchased those half share of the suit land from Upendra Nath Barman by a registered Kabala dated 8-8-1970 and thus she became owner of the entire 57 decimal of land in the suit Khatian No.420 and in the suit Plot No.460. But subsequently, land of this plot was declared Enemy Property by the Government in the year 1969 in Case No.19 (Non- Agricultural land) of 1969-1970. The case was heard on 9-5-1974 and it was dismissed on the same day on finding that the suit property in question was not Enemy Property.

7. The defendant No.1 of the present suit, Nurul Haque, though was a tenant under the plaintiff in some portion of the suit land on rent but took lease of 07 decimal of land from the Government in collaboration with the officers of the Enemy Property Cell. The said enemy property case was sent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dinajpur for order who was pleased to release the entire 57 decimal of land from the list of enemy property on 28-1-1978 after proper hearing. Against that order of release the present defendant No.1 preferred an Appeal being No.14 of 1978 to the learned Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi and upon full hearing the learned Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi was pleased to reject the said Appeal.

8. The plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land by constructing pucca wall, bathroom, latrine and tubewell. She also planted various sorts of fruit bearing trees in the suit plot. She also paid holding taxes regularly in the Municipality and subsequently, transferred 14 decimal of land to several persons on several dates under kabalas and the purchasers are also in possession of the suit land in their respective shares by opening new holding and by paying rent to the Government. The remaining 41 decimal of land has been duly recorded in the name of the plaintiff and the defendants including the defendant No.1 have no right, title and possession in the suit land.

The defendant No.1 has obtained an ex parte decree from the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 after he was defeated in the VP Miscellaneous Caseie after release of the suit property and got the ex parte decree behind the knowledge of the plaintiff, in respect of 19 decimal of land on 24-5-1979. The plaintiff was not made a party in that suit intentionally and her title has been clouded by that ex parte decree and thus, she has been obliged to institute the instant suit.

9. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have submitted two separate written statements and contested the suit. In his written statements the defendant No.1 stated that the plaintiff has no cause of action to file the suit nor locus standi for it. The suit is barred by law of limitation and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and also by the principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence and that the .suit land originally belonged to one Subarna Probha Biswas who after the partition of the sub-continent has left for India. During the SA operation, the suit land was recorded in the name of one Hanuman Das Agarwala as forceful occupier of the suit plot who is also the defendant No.3 in the instant suit. The story of the Certificate Case No.153/1958-59 and the auction purchase or delivery of possession thereof, are all false and collusive and mere paper transactions. The plaintiff and defendant No.3, namely, Hanuman Das Agarwala, have never acquired any right, title and possession in the suit land by that auction. The suit that was instituted by Upendra Nath i-e the Partition Suit No.4 of 1963, was false for, no summons was served upon him in the suit. The plaintiff also instituted the Suit No.37 of 1966 challenging the title of Upendra Nath in the Partition Suit No.4 of 1963 where the husband of the present plaintiff admitted that the defendant No.3 Hanuman Das Agarwala had been in possession of the suit land before the initiation of the Certificate Case No.153 of 1958-59 and, as such, the plaintiffs averments that the defendant No.3 has no possession in the suit land is false. He has erected houses about 17/18 years ago in the suit plot, when it was covered by bushes and fallen land. A holding was opened in the Municipality in his name and he got receipts of payment of taxes. He has constructed houses on 7 (seven) decimal of land about 16/17 years ago within the full knowledge of the plaintiff and her husband and also the defendant No.3. He also possesses an area of excess 12 decimal of land adjacent to his house and, as such, he is in the possession of 12 + 7 = 19 decimals of land and thus, has acquired a good title by his adverse possession. He was never a tenant under the plaintiff. The plaintiff may have purchased 28.5 decimal of land from Upendra Nath on the basis of a collusive decree that he got in the Partition Suit No.4 of 1963, but has acquired no title on the basis of that collusive decree. The plaintiff was not affected by the decree passed in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978. No party was left out in that Other Class Suit and the plaintiff is bound by that decree. The plaintiff neither has possession nor homestead in the suit land as alleged and the authority i.e, the Government, at one point of time, advised him to take lease of his homestead measuring an area of 7 decimal ofland from the Government failing which, they will evict him therefrom and finding no other alternative, he took lease of 7 decimal of land under compulsion and thus, he retained possession of 19 decimal of land. He instituted the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 for declaration of his title as he has acquired his good title by virtue of his long standing adverse possession and got an ex parte decree in it. He also applied for mutation of his decretal land and then came to learn that the husband of the plaintiff has applied for demarcation of 16 decimal of land and the plaintiffs husband also tried to enter into the suit land with the help of the local wicked and dangerous people on 18-1-1980. The defendant with his sons have resisted them and also filed a criminal case, being No. MP 18/1980 which was subsequently renumbered as MR Case No.19/1980 in which the husband of the plaintiff and his men have been restrained from entering into the suit land under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on 12-2-1980.

10. The defendant No.2, has, on the other hand, stated that he is not bound by the decree obtained by the defendant No.1 and that the suit land originally belonged to one Suburna Probha Biswas who was in possession and subsequently, left for India leaving the property uncared for. No auction was held as alleged. The PRR Khatian was prepared in the name of Subarna Probha, but subsequently, it was recorded in the name of Hanuman Das Agarwala as forceful occupier. The record was prepared in the name of Suborna Probha under section 46 and it was correct. The ex parte decree obtained by the defendant No.1 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 is collusive one between the defendant No.1 and the plaintiff and Upendra Nath. The defendant is not bound by the decree of the defendant No.1.

11. During the re-trial of the suit on remand, learned Munsif has framed two issues, namely, whether the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and barred by limitation for the learned appellate Court has directed to decide those two points in its order of remand and the learned trial Court held that the plaintiff has proved her title in the entire land but the defendant No.1, Nurul Haque is in possession of 19 sataks of land and the plaintiff failed to prove that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land' as tenant of the plaintiff. She did not produce any deed of tenancy agreement or rent receipts in this respect and her witnesses are partisan and their evidence are not reliable to the effect that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land as tenant of the plaintiff.

12. On perusal of the document namely, the tax paying receipt of the Municipality of the year 1965, produced by the defendant No.1, the learned trial Court held that the defendant No.1 is in possession of that 19 sataks of land from 15/16 years ago. In accordance with the auction purchase dated 12-12- 1960. the plaintiff got possession in the southern portion or the suit plot and she could not explain as to how she got possession in 28'/2 steaks of land in the northern portion of the plot. By auction. Hanuman Das Agarwala got possession of this plot which he sold out to Upendra Nath Barman by a registered deed. Upendra Nath Barman instituted the Partition Suit praying for separate shaham where he lost upto appeal and, on the contrary, he won the Title Suit upto the appellate Court and in that Partition Suit this defendant No.1 was also a defendant. From that period this defendant is an illegal occupier in the suit land and his possession is adverse to all and continuous. The plaintiff has purchased from Upendra Nath Barman on 8-8-1970 by a registered deed measuring an area of 28-1/2 sataks in the northern portion of the plot but she could not prove acquiring her possession under the Kabala. The plaintiff also could not prove whether her vendor Upendra Nath Barman executed the decree which he obtained in his Partition Suit. The title of the plaintiff in the suit land is mere paper title and that she inserted her claim for recovery of possession on 29-9-1984 by way of amendment of the plaint. It could not be said that the possession of the defendant No.1 was not adverse to the plaintiff only because he took lease of it from the Government as Enemy Property. The defendant No.1 has enjoyed adverse possession and right, title thereof from 1963 to 1984. Though the ex parte decree was passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 without making the plaintiff a party and in her absence, but still it can be said that the decree was passed on finding his possession. The plaintiff has lost her cause of action by not suing from 8-8-1970. to 29-9-1984 and the suit is barred by section 144 of the Limitation Act. But the suit is maintainable in its nature and form. The suit is not hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

13. In the Other Suit No. 18 of 1980, the Learned Munsif held that the defendant No.2. i-e, the Government, could not produce any documentary evidence to prove that the suit land is an Enemy Property and the activities of the defendant No. 1 are not clean. From the volume of the SA Khatian the Suit Plot No.46D was found recorded in the name of Subarna Prova. The defendant No.1 has committed wrong in obtaining the ex parte decree. The plaintiff has good title over the suit land and her interests has been clouded by the ex parte decree. It was thus, not binding upon the plaintiff.

14. The findings of the Learned Appellate Court in the Other Appeal No. 19 of 1992, on the contrary, are that as soon as the defendant No.1 took lease of 7 decimal of land from the Government as Enemy Property, his claim of adverse possession stood relinquished and, as such, the limitation of more than 12 years has been completed. The findings of the learned trial Court on the point of limitation was erroneous. The defendant No. 1 has not acquired any title by adverse possession and he is liable to eviction. The defendant No.1 claimed that he is dwelling in an area of 0.07 sataks of land having his dwelling house and possessing another 12 sataks of contiguous land by growing vegetables and plantation which is a new claim, not raised in the Other Suit No. 100 of 1978.

15. Mr Mahbubey Alam appearing with Mrs Mafuza Begum, the learned Advocates, for the petitioner, has advanced mainly threefold arguments: namely, (a) the plaintiff by adducing oral and documentary evidence could not prove the date of her alleged dispossession from the suit land. Relying upon the cases of Jogendra Nath alias Govinda Sarker vs Amulya Chandra Sarker and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 147. Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 100, the learned Advocate submits that since the plaintiff failed to prove induction of the defendant No.1 as her tenant in the suit land, he will be treated under the law, as a hostile possessor and his possession is adverse possession under the law; (b) With reference to the cases of Radhamoni Debi vs Collector and others reported in 27 Indian Appeals 136, Secretary of State vs Debendra Lal, reported in 1934 (Privy Council) 23; Ejas Ali Qidwai and others vs Special Manager. Court of Wards. Balrampur Estate and others reported in 1935 (Privy Council) 53 and Musa Ali vs Nur Ahmed and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 154 the Learned Advocate submits that since the possession of the defendant No.1 was open, overt, continuous and competitive against his competitor, the same has conferred a good title against all except the real owner and since the defendant No.1 has proved by evidence that he is in possession of the suit land the onus of proof was shifted upon the plaintiff to prove that he was inducted by her as her tenant or was her permissive possessor or licensee and in the absence of such proof: the possession of the defendant No.1 is clearly an adverse possession and (c) the defendant No.1 is in possession of the suit land from 1963 without break as it was found by the Courts below and so he has acquired his title in the suit land by way of adverse possession and the Learned appellate Court has erred in law in not holding title in the suit land by adverse possession and the findings and conclusion of the learned appellate Court is liable to be set aside.

16. Mr Md Fazlul Karim with Mr ABM Mahbub, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party, submits on the other hand, that the suit property was declared Enemy Property in the year 1969 and it remained as such till its release in favour of the plaintiff in the year 1978 and the defendant No.1 got lease of 7 sataks of land from the Government acknowledging and admitting the property to be the property of the Government and thus this period running from 1969-78 could not be added to or deemed to be hostile or adverse possession against the plaintiff. The learned Courts below found that the defendant No.1 has entered into an unlawful possession in 1963 and since the property was declared Enemy Property in 1969 his possession was of only 6 years prior to declaration of Enemy Property. The suit was instituted in 1980 and; as such, the period of his possession is not more than 8 years in all and, as such, he has acquired no adverse possession or title in the suit land. The plaintiff need not prove her constructive possession, since the possession of the defendant No.1 was broken. The defendant No.1 cannot claim his adverse possession in the suit land as was held by their Lordships in the case of Kumar Basanta Roy and others vs Secretary of Stale for India in Council and others reported in 44 Indian Appeals 104.

17. Perused the application, heard the learned Advocates and considered their submissions.

18. There is no statutory definition of adverse possession. The limitation of adverse possession is a matter of practice ascribed to sections 26 and 27 of the Limitation Act which is also not categorical. From different textbooks and judicial pronouncements it appears that adverse possession comprises of possession (a) commenced in wrong; and (b) maintained against a right.

19. It has been variously described eg, (a) abnormal enjoyment. against all the world, but wrongly against the true owner (b) continuous possession against the title of the true owner if continued for the statutory period of limitation except making re-entry or bringing an action (c) Continuous exercise of right or title against the true owner which cannot afterwards be refused, either by re-entry or subsequent acknowledgment (Pannamma Velly vs Achu Thana Union. ILR 1966, 1 Kerala 689). Possession by continuous assertion against the title of the dispossessed owner and actual exclusive possession of the property commenced and continued to a clear right either openly or by a void claim' against a constructive claim adverse against the competitor and actual in continuity, in publicity and to the extent to show that its possession is adverse to the competitor.

Since title by adverse possession is relating to the possession which is not legal and obtained in some unlawful manner and by continuity for specific period, the person concerned is claiming title thereupon, it must be categorical and specific.

<u>20. In acquisition of ownership the maxim "qui prior est tempore potior est Jure" (whoever is prior in point of time has priority in law) applies. So, where two rights or title conflict the earlier prevails unless there be some reason to prefer the latter. Ownership is distinct from possession.</u>

<u>Ownership is de jure recognition of a claim to certain property. Possession is the objective realisation of ownership. It is the de facto exercise of a claim to certain property and a de facto counterpart of ownership. Possession is a right in the de facto relation of continuing exercise and enjoyment as opposed to the de jure relation of ownership. Possession is thus external form to justify and normally manifest in the possession in fact. Possession denotes the relationship between a person: (a) some actual power over the object possessed. i.e. physical (corporeal) control or actual possession; and (b) some amount of will to avail oneself of that power that is the desire to possess (animus). Thus, it expresses the physical relation of control exercised by a person over the thing. The possessor may be or may not be the owner of the thing. Possession confers more than a personal right to be protected against wrongdoers. It confers a qualified right to possess, a right in the nature of property which is valid against everybody who cannot show a prior or better right. The law under such circumstances assists not only the possessor himself but also those who stand in the place of the possessor by succession or transfer. The term dispossession, on the other hand, is, in essence, ouster of possession. The prefix of the term "dis" is "negative", "objection", "separation" and "deprivation". The dictionary meaning of the term "dispossession" is "to be out of possession from acquired or right of property. " In the case of Basanta Kumar Roy vs Secretary of State, reported in LR 44 of 104, their Lordships held that "the meaning of 'dispossession' is well settled. A man may cease to use his land because he cannot use it, since it is under water. He does not thereby discontinue his possession. Constructively, his possession continues until he is dispossessed: and upon the cessation of the dispossession before the lapse of the statutory period, constructively, it revives."</u>

21. In the case permissive possession is also an issue for the plaintiff claimed that the defendant No.1 has entered into the possession of the suit land as her tenant and remained there as her permissive possessor. Permissive possession does not amount to dispossession. If the person in permissive possession changes his animus and continued to hold continuous assertion of hostile title openly the possession becomes adverse to the owner after expiry of specific period of limitation. A trespasser, on the other hand, if continues in possession for the statutory period, the adverse possession is created, which may be covered by title of the trespasser, if the conditions of adverse possession are satisfied. Trespass means to enter into land or a building that does not have permission or the right to enter. Trespasser's possession is only unlawful possession and mere unlawful possession does not mean adverse possession.

A trespasser's possession becomes adverse only when the adverse nature of trespasser's claim entered into the knowledge of the true owner. Trespass literally means wrongful disturbance of another person's possession of immovable property by entering upon the premises in the possession of another or remaining upon such premises.

In order to make the possession adverse, it has to be proved on the part of the trespasser his explicit possession exclusive to the true owner.

In the case of Bush vs Smith, (1953) 6 PL 670 their Lordships held that: "Neither the use of force, nor the breaking of an enclosure or transgression of a visible boundary, nor even an unlawful intention, is necessary to constitute an actionable trespass." And in the case of Lawrence vs Tucker, (1938) 160 Ore 474: 85 it was held that: "The motive of the intruder is immaterial and the trespass cannot be justified even by showing that it resulted in a benefit to the occupier."

<u>22. On the other hand, the term licence has been defined in section 60 of the Easement Act meaning a licence to property is based on trust which makes the action lawful, which without it, would have been unlawful.</u>

<u>In the case of Play Fair vs Musgrove, 153 ER, 465 their Lordships held that: "A licensee must quit upon the termination of the licence and if he overstayed, he became a trespasser,"</u>

<u>Therefore, licensee means, In essence, possession or enjoyment, without passing any interest in the property to which it relates, which could be otherwise wrongful.</u>

23. In the instant case, admittedly the property belonged to one Subarna Probha and according to the plaintiff, the property was auction sold and she, together with one Hanuman Das Agarwala (defendant No.3) purchased that property in the auction proceeding and got possession thereof through the Court and subsequently, Hanuman Das sold out his share to one Upendra Nath who instituted a suit praying for his separate saham and he lost the suit upto appeal. He then instituted a Title Suit and obtaining a decree and won up to appeal. The plaintiff purchased the share of Upendra Nath, after being lost in that Title Suit and appeal, by her kabala and became owner of the entire property, in question. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the story of Certificate Case and Auction Sale of the suit property and purchase of the plaintiff are all false. Subarna Probha was the owner and possessor of the suit property and in the Khatian Hanuman Das was recorded as forceful possessor. When Subarna Probha left for' India sometime around the partition of the subcontinent, he got his possession in the property by making a house in the portion where Hanuman Das was the forceful possessor. Subarna Probha's property became Enemy Property and was listed as such in the year 1969 and he got lease of .07 sataks of land from the Government in whom the property was vested and in this area of land he has his homestead and the lease continued till its release in 1978.

The plaintiff has asserted her right from the proceeding of the certificate case, particularly after her purchase on auction. She had been involved in litigations in respect of the suit land where Hanuman Das got his possession followed by Upendra Nath and thereafter, by the Government and, last of all, the present defendant No.1.

The learned appellate Court found that the plaintiff's persuasion and chase to the equal share holder of Certificate purchase, Hanuman Das, has finally led to the point of her purchase from Upendra Nath. Upon purchase of the property in auction, the plaintiff got possession in the southern half and Hanuman Das in the northern half of the suit plot. While the plaintiff was trying to come to the northern half of the land in question by way of litigations with Hanuman Das he made an exit by way of transfer to Upendra Nath and Upendra Nath was in possession of this portion. From Upendra Nath the plaintiff has finally purchased it and Upendra Nath had his right, title and possession therein.

The learned first trial Court also found possession of the defendant No.1, but since the defendant No.1 could not explain his possession, the Learned Court held that it will not amount as hostile to the plaintiff. In the opinion of the learned remand Court, since before her purchase from Upendra Nath., the defendant No.1 was possessing the half share of Hanuman Das, so his possession was prior to the purchase of the plaintiff. It is hostile against Hanuman Das and also against the plaintiff. Though the plaintiff acquired title, but she did not get the possession of it.

In arriving at the aforesaid findings the Learned Courts below committed a grave omission in not looking into the fact, why Upendra Nath lost his Partition Suit upto its appeal against the present plaintiff and why he was compelled to institute a Title Suit instead: especially, why his prayer for separate saham was refused.

24. The other important factor in this case is the interruption. While the litigations were going on between the plaintiff and Hanuman Das or between the plaintiff and Upendra Nath, suddenly, the Government has entered into the scene and taken away the suit property declaring it Enemy Property. After its release from the list of Enemy Property, it again came back to the plaintiff, giving rise to the question as to with whom the possession remained during this period.

<u>25. The plaintiff has taken the plea of permissive possession. Plaintiff's possession, according to her, is one, where a true owner is neither dispossessed nor discontinued the possession because a third person has taken away the possession. But whether such a possession constitutes an adverse possession, is a mixed question of law and facts.</u>

<u>In a case of acquiring title by adverse possession, the possessor has to remain in an uninterrupted possession for the full period of 12 years. If the adverse dispossession discontinued, for however short a time before he completes his title, his previous possession loses its value. In Kumar Basanta Roy's Case. (Supra) their Lordships held that "where the Government after taking possession of re-formed lands has released them to persons claiming to be entitled, those persons do not derive their liability to be sued from or through the Government within the meaning of section 3 of the Act and upon a claim to possession they consequently cannot rely under Article 144 upon the period during which the Government had possession."</u>

<u>In the case of Thakur Singh vs Bhogeraj Singh, 'reported in ILR 27 (Cal) 29 their Lordships held that "in order to acquire title by adverse possession, the possession must not only be open and exclusive, but it must also be shown to have been adverse for the full statutory period i-e, it must be continuous for the full period (without any break or without interruption)." And as per decision given in the case of Badri vs Smt. Ram Rati, 1977 RD (BR) 224, it was held that the claimant has to specifically show his possession from year to year, particularly so, if he is a trespasser by continuity. " (also the case of Gouri Sanker vs Deputy Director, Consolidation, 1980 RD 250 continuity not found, presumption not drawn). In another case of Ganda Singh and others vs Ram Narain Singh, reported in AIR 1959 (Punjab) 147 it was held that "the claimant must show on what date he came into possession, what was the nature of his possession, whether the factum of his possession was known to the legal claimants and how long his possession continued."</u>

26. In the instant case, both the plaintiff and defendant No.1 have abstained from stating on what date the defendant No.1 came into possession and both of them have intelligently avoided the point of time on what date the defendant No.1 entered upon possession, in the suit land. In such a case, priority of possession is also relevant and the point was considered by their Lordships in the, case of Ramchandra Apaji vs Balaji Bhaurav, reported in ILR 9 (Bombay) 137 holding that "it is not difficult to find out where the plaintiff has been affected and deprived of certain property belonged to her for the defendant has wrong possession over it. The question is one of the title or ownership in the case and if the plaintiff can establish that she is the owner and the defendant cannot show a better title the latter must go out. The plaintiff may prove her prior possession out of use standing for such long period of time. But all adverse claims by law is subject to limitation."

27. In the instant case, the plaintiff is claiming possession by virtue of her ownership and by way of purchase from Upendra and even prior to it by virtue of her litigations with Hanuman Das on the point of share and possession and the defendant is claiming his wrongful possession based without any ante-dated deed and in view of the above decisions, the title holder shall have the priority.

28. Upendra Nath Das, the vendor of the plaintiff, has appeared in the suit as PW 2 supporting the plaintiffs possession in the suit land. The PW 3 Shahadat Hossain has completed his evidence by saying that he is also carrying on business in the suit land under the plaintiff and the plaintiff is possessing the suit land by growing fruit bearing trees, etc. The defendant No.1, on the other hand, has produced no other oral evidence except himself. But facts remain that his claim of possession has not been corroborated by any corroborative evidence, especially about the starting point of his possession. It is on record that the Government has interrupted his continuous possession that was adverse, according to him, to the title and possession of the plaintiff, for the period of 1969-78 and in view of the cases referred to above, the possession must be uninterrupted to acquire title to the property by adverse possession.

29. Mr Mahbubey Alam has relied upon the case of Jogendra Nath vs Amulya Chandra Sarker and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 147. But the dispute arose in that case was out of a Will and extinction of title on the basis of will by adverse possession.

He has also relied upon the case of Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 100. But in that case, the defendant took the plea of tenancy and encroachment.

He has relied upon another of Musa Ali vs Nur Ahmed and another [44 DLR (AD) 154] and this case is on the point of limitation.

I find these cases are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

30. In the case of Nazira Begum vs Roushanara Begum, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 22 their Lordships held that "onus of proof is upon the defendant and apparent show of possession is not sufficient. Constructive possession is not equal possession. In the case of tenancy in common ownership are not examined."

In the case of Madaris Ali and others vs Biswamber Das, reported in 46 DLR 34 their Lordships held that "evidence of forcible entry in the suit land, cannot amount to adverse possession."

31. In view of the above, I find that the petitioner, Md Nurul Haque has not acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession, especially by virtue of his unspecified and interrupted possession. He is mere a trespasser, who acquired no title.

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 27-7-1993, decree signed on 31-5- 1993 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon, in Title Appeal No.19 of 1992, reversing the judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992, decree signed on 3-6-1992, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Thakurgaon, in Other Suit No. 5 of 1985 is hereby upheld.

Send down the lower Court's Record at once.

End.
